title: Mangroves, Wetlands and Biosphere Reserves of India

cards.b:
Biosphere reserves, wetlands and mangroves are standard prelims facts and mains themes about conservation. Each sits in a legal and international framework. Know the numbers, the largest examples and the way each is protected.

The three topics belong together: mangroves and wetlands are habitats, while biosphere reserves are a management category that can contain both. Learn the number, place and law for each.

Salt-tolerant forests of tidal coasts. Features: pneumatophores (breathing roots), prop roots, viviparous seeds, salt glands. They stabilise shores, buffer cyclones and tsunamis, and store blue carbon. India's mangrove area is about 4,992 sq km (ISFR 2021), about 0.15 percent of the land. West Bengal (Sundarbans) has the largest cover, then Gujarat, then Andaman and Nicobar.

Common species: Rhizophora, Avicennia, Sonneratia, and Heritiera fomes (sundari) in the Sundarbans. Other sites: Bhitarkanika (Odisha), Godavari-Krishna delta, Pichavaram (Tamil Nadu). Threats: aquaculture ponds, reclamation, sand mining and oil pollution. Protected by the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ-I). The MISHTI scheme (2023) promotes planting.

The Sundarbans is a mangrove delta in both India and Bangladesh. It is a Ramsar site, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1987) and a tiger reserve of the Royal Bengal tiger.

A wetland holds water over land, for part or all of the year. The Ramsar Convention (Iran, 1971) lists wetlands of international importance. India joined in 1982. As of 2024 India had over 80 Ramsar sites, among the highest in Asia (check the latest count). Examples: Chilika (first, 1981), Keoladeo, Loktak, Sundarbans, Wular, Sambhar, Ashtamudi, Vembanad, Harike.

The Montreux Record lists Ramsar sites facing damage. In India, Loktak is on it; Chilika was listed and then removed in 2002. The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 replaced the 2010 rules and shifted powers to states. The National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA) funds work.

A biosphere reserve (BR) follows UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere programme (1971). It has three zones: core (strict protection), buffer (limited research and eco-friendly use) and transition (people live and work). India has 18 BRs, of which 12 are in the UNESCO network.

India's first: Nilgiri (1986). Other BRs: Nanda Devi, Nokrek, Manas, Sundarbans, Gulf of Mannar, Great Nicobar, Simlipal, Dibru-Saikhowa, Dehang-Debang, Pachmarhi, Achanakmar-Amarkantak, Kachchh, Cold Desert, Seshachalam, Panna, Agasthyamala, Khangchendzonga.

• Nilgiri: Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka.
  • Agasthyamala: Kerala, Tamil Nadu.
  • Sundarbans: West Bengal.
  • Gulf of Mannar: Tamil Nadu (marine).
  • Cold Desert: Himachal Pradesh (Spiti).
  • Nokrek: Meghalaya.
  • Simlipal: Odisha.
  • Pachmarhi: Madhya Pradesh.
  • Kachchh: Gujarat, the largest by area.

Local people use mangroves as fuelwood, honey and fish sources. In the Sundarbans, honey collectors and fishermen face tiger attacks, which is why compensation and tiger-proof fencing are policy topics.

Core areas often displace forest dwellers. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises rights, but conflict persists over critical wildlife habitats. Advocates of 'fortress conservation' say people harm wildlife, while advocates of community conservation point to sacred groves and community reserves that work well.

Sacred groves, such as the Khasi groves in Meghalaya and the kavus in Kerala, show community conservation. Community reserves were added to the Wildlife Act by the 2002 amendment.

National parks (stricter), wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves, community reserves, all under the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972. Biosphere reserves are not a legal category under this Act; they are an administrative designation. Ramsar sites also need no separate legal status, though many sit inside parks.

A national park prohibits grazing and private rights, while a biosphere reserve has zones for people. Wildlife sanctuaries allow some human activity under rules. UNESCO designates BRs, but the country keeps control.

Likely questions: 'Role of mangroves in coastal protection', 'What are biosphere reserves and how do they differ from national parks?', 'Ramsar sites in India'.

  • Distinguish zones and use.
  • Give three examples each with states.
  • Link to blue carbon, cyclone buffers and livelihoods.

India also has Ramsar sites in Punjab (Harike, Kanjli), Kerala (Sasthamkotta), Jammu and Kashmir (Wular, Hokera) and Manipur (Loktak). Keep a state-wise map of ten sites in mind for prelims.
